note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The distractor 'Dust from the site settles on land and never reaches it' uses 'never', but the card says sites 'can' send dust and runoff into waterways. The absolute word makes this option easy to rule out without knowing the idea.

rejected.title: Mining and urban development
card: Mining and quarrying
Mines and quarries dig out rock, coal, metals or sand. This can remove hills or whole sections of a landform and leave large pits.
Urban development
New suburbs are built on cleared land. Trees and grass are removed, the ground is levelled, and roads and roofs cover the soil.
Both clear the vegetation that covered the land. Without it, dust and loose soil can blow or wash away.

Mines can pollute water and air around them, for example with dust or with chemicals that run off into creeks. Building sites and new suburbs can also send dirty runoff and dust into nearby waterways and the air.
rejected.remember: Mining and new suburbs reshape land by removing landforms and vegetation, and can pollute water and air nearby.

a.q: Which change to a landscape is most likely when a quarry opens beside a hill?
opts: Part of the hill is dug away and its vegetation is removed
The hill grows taller because quarrying adds new rock to it
More trees grow on the hill because the soil is loosened
The hill is left unchanged but the nearby river dries up
a.why: A quarry digs out rock and clears the plants that grew there, so part of the landform is removed. Quarrying takes rock out rather than adding it, and nothing in the card says digging helps trees grow.
a.clue: Think about what a quarry takes out of the ground.

b.q: A new suburb is built on bushland near a creek in Perth. Builders clear the trees and level the ground. What is a likely effect on the creek?
opts: Dirty runoff from the building site washes into it
The creek is cleaner because there are fewer trees
The creek is unaffected because the land is flat
Dust from the site settles on land and never reaches it
b.why: Clearing trees and levelling ground leaves loose soil and dust, which rain can wash into nearby waterways. Flat ground does not stop this runoff, and dust from building sites can reach both waterways and the air.
b.clue: Bare soil is easy for rain to carry away.

a.q: Which change to a landscape is most likely when a quarry opens beside a hill?
opts: Part of the hill is dug away and its vegetation is removed
The hill grows taller as dug material is piled on it
More trees grow on the hill because the soil is loosened
The hill is left unchanged but the nearby river dries up
a.why: A quarry digs out rock and clears the plants that grew there, so part of the landform is removed. Piling material on the hill is not the main effect, and nothing in the card says digging helps trees grow.
a.clue: Think about what a quarry takes out of the ground.

b.q: A new suburb is built on bushland near a creek in Perth. Builders clear the trees and level the ground. What is a likely effect on the creek?
opts: Dirty runoff from the building site washes into it
The creek is cleaner because there are fewer trees
The creek is unaffected because the land is flat
The creek fills with water because roofs add rainfall
b.why: Clearing trees and levelling ground leaves loose soil and dust, which can wash into nearby waterways. Flat ground does not protect a creek, and roofs do not add rainfall, they only cover the soil.
b.clue: Bare soil is easy for rain to carry away.

a.best: Part of the hill is dug away and its vegetation is removed

b.best: Dirty runoff from the building site washes into it

problems.detail: Why (b) says roofs 'only cover the soil'. Roofs and roads are hard surfaces that send more stormwater, and send it faster, into nearby creeks. Saying they only cover the soil could teach students that hard surfaces have no effect on creek flow. The distractor itself is still wrong, because roofs do not add rainfall.
